model.name: 1% + Hard Pity 100
model.blurb: A 1% chase rate with hard pity at 100. No rate ramp or 50/50.
model.source: A textbook 1% geometric drop rate with a hard cap. Useful as a baseline for comparing rate ramps and featured guarantees.
notes: Without pity, a 1% drop takes 100 pulls on average. Guaranteeing it by pull 100 cuts the long tail and brings the average below 100.
There is no 50/50: every chase-rarity hit is the featured prize.

overview.summary: This is a fictional character-collection game stripped down to one easy rule: each draw has a 1% chance of the chase reward, and draw 100 guarantees it if it has not appeared. There is no licensed game or player community behind this example. It is a clean starting point for trying a new gacha idea without also changing a complicated roster or economy.
overview.distinctive: The chance stays the same until the guaranteed draw. There are no rising odds or extra checkpoints to learn, so any change in player waits is easier to connect to a rule you edited.
overview.strength: A clear maximum gives the player a saving target. The design tradeoff is that the draws before it may feel repetitive: the guarantee improves certainty, but does not by itself make the rewards exciting.
overview.analysis: Try an earlier guarantee, rising late-draw odds or a different base chance. Compare the typical wait with the experience of the unluckiest players, rather than judging the system by the average alone.
overview.popularity: This is a teaching example, not a released game. It has no measured audience, review score, retention result or sales history. Use it to compare design choices, then validate the promising ones with players.
overview.business: In a paid implementation, extra draws could be sold through currency packs; in a free implementation, tickets could come entirely from play. Neither is assumed to be profitable here. Price, earned ticket supply, content appeal and operating costs would decide the business outcome.
